classification.difficultyReason: Classify the variables by their possible values, then connect that distinction to face counts and height intervals while recognising that all height readings come from the same student.

content.prompt: A six-sided die is rolled, and the height of a randomly chosen student (measured in centimetres) is recorded.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Identify and justify which random variable is discrete and which is continuous.

answer.short: The die result is discrete because it has six possible values. Height is continuous because it can take any value within a range.
answer.worked: The die result takes one of the separate values $1,2,3,4,5,6$, so it is discrete. Height can take intermediate values between any two heights in its range, so it is continuous. The precision of the recording only limits the values written down.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Suppose the die is rolled 50 times and the student’s height is measured 50 times. Discuss how the frequency distributions of these variables would look different when graphed.

answer.short: The die results have a separate bar for each face. A histogram of the height measurements would show frequencies concentrated near the same student’s height.
answer.worked: A frequency bar chart for the die has separate positions for faces 1 to 6. For a fair die, the six frequencies are expected to be roughly similar, with variation from one set of 50 rolls to another. A histogram groups heights into adjacent intervals. Since the same student is measured each time, the measurements would usually be identical to the recording precision or cluster around the student's height. Identical recorded measurements would all fall in one interval.
